text_blocks.snippet: Potassium-lowering medications, also known as potassium binders, are used to treat hyperkalemia, a condition where there is too much potassium in the blood. These medications work by binding to potassium in the digestive tract, preventing its absorption into the bloodstream, and then helping the body eliminate the excess potassium through bowel movements.

list.title: Sodium Zirconium Cyclosilicate (Lokelma):
list.snippet: This medication binds to potassium in the gastrointestinal tract, reducing its absorption and promoting its removal through feces.

list.title: Patiromer (Veltassa):
list.snippet: A non-absorbed, cation exchange polymer that increases fecal potassium excretion by binding to potassium in the digestive tract.

list.title: Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate (Kayexalate):
list.snippet: An exchange resin that binds to potassium in the intestines, exchanging it for sodium, and is used for mild to moderate hyperkalemia.

text_blocks.snippet: Other medications that can affect potassium levels:

list.snippet: Insulin: Can lower potassium levels by driving it into cells.
Beta2 agonists (like albuterol): Can also lower potassium levels by a similar mechanism to insulin.
Loop diuretics (like furosemide and bumetanide): Can increase potassium excretion through the kidneys.
Corticosteroids: Can increase potassium excretion through the kidneys.

list.title: Not for emergencies:
list.snippet: Patiromer and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate are not intended for the immediate treatment of life-threatening hyperkalemia due to their delayed onset of action, according to Medscape.

list.title: Side effects:
list.snippet: Common side effects of potassium binders include abdominal pain, bloating, constipation, diarrhea, gas, heartburn, indigestion, nausea, and vomiting.

list.title: Monitoring:
list.snippet: It is crucial to monitor potassium levels regularly while taking these medications to ensure they are effective and to prevent hypokalemia (low potassium).
